{"category":"RTG specific power","notes":"v1.9.0.  The nuclear counterpart to 'Power system specific mass', and the reason it is a separate row: this one does NOT scale with heliocentric distance.\nGPHS-RTG (Cassini, New Horizons, Galileo): 290 We at 56 kg = 5.2 W/kg.  MMRTG (Curiosity, Perseverance): 110 We at 44 kg = 2.5 W/kg (NASA OIG IG-23-010 Table 1), worse because it is qualified to run in an atmosphere as well as vacuum.  5.0 W/kg takes the deep-space-only design.\nThe crossover against the 60 W/kg-at-1-AU solar row is at sqrt(60/5) = 3.46 AU: inside that, PV is lighter per watt; outside it, nothing beats a radioisotope.  RTGs cost ~625\u00d7 more per watt ($500k vs $800), so the model buys the smallest one that does the job, which is exactly how real outer-planet missions are sized.  Supply is the real constraint and it is NOT priced here: 1.5 kg/yr is DOE's Pu-238 production GOAL for 2026, and actual output 2018-2021 was 0.77 kg against 1.5 kg planned (NASA OIG IG-23-010). A rig anchored to a rotating body stands on a surface that is lit half the time, by geometry — the same 0.50 STORAGE_REFERENCE has carried since v1.9.0, moved here so Module 4 can actually read it.  Ranges below 0.5 for a high-latitude or near-polar emplacement on a body with obliquity, above it for an equatorial site with local horizon shadowing.
This is a SIZING factor, not a specific mass, and that is why no W/kg figure can absorb it: to deliver P continuously through a dark fraction f you must INSTALL P·[(1−f) + f/η_rt]/(1−f) of generating capacity, because the sunlit hours have to run the load and recharge the store as well.  At f = 0.50 and η_rt = 0.90 that is 2.11×.
The alternative architecture is to mine at half duty cycle and take twice the stay time instead; Module 4 sizes the storage rather than halving the duty, which is the choice that leaves mission duration comparable across bodies.
Does NOT apply to a radioisotope source — an RTG's output is flat — and does not apply to the electric-propulsion array, which is in interplanetary cruise and in permanent sunlight.","range_high":0.55,"range_low":0.35,"reference_year":2026,"unit":"fraction of the time a surface rig sees no sun","value":0.5}

value: {"category":"Energy storage usable specific energy","notes":"v1.11.0.  130 Wh/kg at the system level (STORAGE_REFERENCE 'Li-ion battery (system level)': cells reach 250-300 Wh/kg and packaging, harness, balancing and thermal roughly halve it) \u00d7 0.80 depth of discharge = 104 Wh/kg USABLE.  NASA's Li-ion state of the art is 175 Wh/kg at 80% depth of discharge and 90% charge/discharge efficiency (Schmitz et al., IEEE Aerospace 2023, NTRS 20230001487, Table 3), so the 0.80 matches and the usable figure there is 140 Wh/kg; this row's 104 is 26% below it.  The 130 Wh/kg system figure has no source of its own.  Cells: ~265 Wh/kg (Ali et al., Frontiers in Energy Research, 2023).  DoD is folded in here rather than carried as a fourth row because a consumer that forgets to apply it silently oversizes the mission by 25%, and this table's job is to hand Module 4 the number it should divide by.\nA regenerative fuel cell (400 Wh/kg, TRL 5) is the obvious architecture for a multi-hour dark period and would cut this term by ~4\u00d7; it is not taken, because nothing has flown one and this row is the operational choice.  The ~4\u00d7 is on storage mass only: NASA's 100 W demonstration measured 47.4% round trip (NASA/TM-20205000357, Table III), so at f = 0.50 the array oversize rises from 2.11\u00d7 to 3.11\u00d7 and part of the saving is paid back in array.","range_high":160.0,"range_low":70.0,"reference_year":2026,"unit":"usable Watt-hours per kg of storage system","value":104.0}

This is the term that makes the array oversize worse than the naive 1/(1\u2212f): the energy that goes through the store has to be generated twice over, once for the load and once for the loss.  At f = 0.50 it is the difference between 2.00\u00d7 and 2.11\u00d7.","range_high":0.95,"range_low":0.8,"reference_year":2026,"unit":"fraction of stored energy recovered","value":0.9}

'Power system specific mass' is 60 W/kg SYSTEM-level against ROSA's ~150 W/kg at the wing, and part of that 2.5\u00d7 is a battery \u2014 so some storage is already paid for and only the INCREMENT above it is new.\n0.58 h is the standard LEO eclipse (35 min of a ~92 min orbit), which is the storage duration a conventional deep-space PV train is specified against. value: {"category":"Volatile cargo containment","notes":"v1.11.0.  Water sold at a depot has to still be water when it arrives.  Exposed ice in sunlight at 1 AU sits far above its sublimation threshold and is simply gone over a multi-year cruise; shaded, sealed and blanketed it is stable for decades.  So the charge is a sealed shaded hold \u2014 no power, no cryocooler, but real mass.\nCarried in STORAGE_REFERENCE since v1.9.0 with '\u26a0\ufe0f  NOT modelled in Module 4' on it, and duplicated here because that table is not one Module 4 loads.  It is INCREMENTAL to the 0.15 ore-restraint fraction Module 4 already flies as `return_structure_frac_of_payload`: the hopper holds the cargo, the seal and shade keep the volatile fraction of it from leaving.  That reading is what makes the storage row's own 'heavier than an ore hopper' true at a value below 0.15.\nCharged on WATER only.  (Until 0.12.4 this said 'which is what the citation covers', but the row cites nothing.)  ENGINEERING ESTIMATE: no published source gives the containment mass fraction, or the stability of a passive sealed, shaded water hold over a multi-year cruise.  NASA's long-term storage work (NASA/TM-2011-215988; Plachta et al. 2017) covers cryogenic propellant tanks with zero-boil-off hardware, not a passive water hold. value:
{"category":"Mining system first-of-kind success probability","notes":"v1.8.1.  Probability the excavation and beneficiation chain works once it arrives — separate from the spacecraft surviving the trip.  Counted from the actual flight record of regolith-contact mechanisms rather than from the failures alone, which is what v1.7.0's 0.75 did and it was unfairly harsh:
  SUCCEEDED (10): Apollo 15-17 drills and scoops; Luna 16 / 20 / 24 drills; Stardust aerogel; Phoenix arm (sticky soil delayed delivery but it worked); Curiosity drill (feed mechanism failed 2016, recovered by feed-extended drilling); Hayabusa2 sampler and SCI impactor, both touchdowns clean; OSIRIS-REx TAGSAM, 121.6 g against a 60 g requirement; Perseverance coring drill; Chang'e 5 and 6 drill + scoop.  (The Curiosity entry is Kinnett, Green, Klein & Lin, JPL, Aerospace Mechanisms Symposium 2022: feed stall on sol 1536, first feed-extended sample on sol 2057.  Shapiro et al., Space Mechanisms Lessons Learned Study Vol. II, NASA TM-107047, 1995, sorts flight lessons by mechanism type.  The other entries are not yet cited.)
  PARTIAL (1): Hayabusa — the projectile never fired, but contact dust was still collected and returned.
  FAILED (2): Philae's harpoon pyrotechnics; InSight's HP3 mole, which could not get purchase in Martian regolith.
That is 11/13 = 0.85 counting Hayabusa as the success it ultimately was, or 10/13 = 0.77 counting it as a loss.  0.85 is taken because Hayabusa did return its sample.
The honest caveat is that NONE of these is sustained mining — they are one-shot or short-campaign collections of grams to kilograms, not a rig moving 200 kg/day for years with no maintenance.  0.85 is therefore the demonstrated mechanism rate, and the sustained-operation risk on top of it is carried by the spacecraft MTBF term rather than double-counted here.  Grows with flight heritage — see 'Mining reliability growth exponent'.","range_high":0.95,"range_low":0.7,"reference_year":2026,"unit":"probability the rig works as designed","value":0.85}

value: {"category":"Mining reliability growth exponent","notes":"v1.9.0.  Reliability is not static across a programme \u2014 it grows as failure modes are found and designed out.  The Duane model has failure probability fall as n^(-alpha) with cumulative production (MIL-HDBK-189C, Jun 2011, 5.2.6).  The handbook's Table II gives historical growth rates of 0.27-0.64 for one-shot systems (median 0.47; the mean is printed '.046', evidently 0.46) and 0.23-0.53 for time-based ones (0.34 mean, 0.32 median), and rejects Duane's universal 0.5.  0.30 sits near the bottom of both ranges \u2014 appropriate for hardware that flies once every few years, where each mission is a slow, expensive lesson and there is no test fleet to accelerate the learning.  The 0.10 low end of the range is below every historical figure the handbook gives: a pessimistic sensitivity bound, not a sourced value.  Until 0.6.1 this note credited MIL-HDBK-189 with a 0.3-0.6 'active' and 0.1-0.2 'passive' band; the handbook draws no such split.","range_high":0.6,"range_low":0.1,"reference_year":2026,"unit":"Duane / AMSAA growth parameter (alpha)","value":0.3}

value: {"category":"Mining system mature success probability","notes":"v1.9.0.  Growth is asymptotic, not unbounded \u2014 no amount of flight heritage makes a machine that grinds rock in vacuum certain to work.  0.95 is where mature, high-cycle spacecraft MECHANISMS sit.  The fleet record: of almost 400 satellites launched successfully 1958-1983, about 10% had some deployment anomaly, mostly mechanical (Shapiro et al., Space Mechanisms Lessons Learned Study Vol. I, NASA TM-107046, 1995).  That is a per-satellite anomaly rate, not a per-deployment success rate; the ~97-99% per deployment once given here is an estimate with no source.  A continuously-operating excavator is harder than a one-shot deployment.  Without this ceiling the Duane curve would eventually promise certainty, which no mechanism earns.","range_high":0.99,"range_low":0.85,"reference_year":2026,"unit":"asymptotic ceiling on rig success probability","value":0.95}

Caps how many missions one rig can actually serve, which the old flat amortisation ignored \u2014 you cannot spread a rig across 100 missions of 2 years each.  Bounded by abrasive wear on regolith-contact mechanisms, thermal cycling and radiation, not by propellant.  ISS-class hardware is rated 15-30 years; a machine chewing rock is at the low end.  Whatever life is left when the programme ends is credited back as terminal value.","range_high":30.0,"range_low":5.0,"reference_year":2026,"unit":"years of operation before wear-out","value":15.0}

value: {"category":"Mining rig maximum trips","notes":"v1.12.0.  The SECOND half of rig service life, and the half that was missing: 'Mining rig service life' above is a CALENDAR bound, and calendar time is not what wears out a machine that cuts rock.  Duty cycles are.  A rig sitting idle between campaigns ages slowly; one digging continuously eats cutting surfaces, seals and bearings on unweathered, angular, never-water-rounded regolith.  Module 4 took min(years/stay) alone, so at a short stay one rig served 12 consecutive campaigns on the strength of a number that only ever said it would not corrode meanwhile.  \u26a0\ufe0f  JUDGEMENT, and there is no flight heritage for it \u2014 nothing has ever mined an asteroid twice.  Bracketed from the two nearest analogues, which disagree in the useful direction.  TERRESTRIAL: mobile mining plant reaches major overhaul near 15,000-25,000 operating hours (~2-3 yr of continuous duty, i.e. ~2 campaigns at this model's ~1.25 yr stay) and survives 2-3 rebuilds before the frame is retired \u2014 but every one of those rebuilds happens in a workshop, and there is no workshop at an asteroid.  FLIGHT: every regolith-contact mechanism ever flown was single-campaign by design or failed inside one \u2014 TAGSAM fired once, Philae's harpoons did not fire, InSight's mole never buried itself, and Curiosity's drill lost its feed mechanism partway through its first decade.  5 is therefore already the optimistic reading of both: rebuild-interval life, achieved un-rebuilt.  range_low 2 is one overhaul interval; range_high 12 restores the pre-v1.12.0 behaviour, where the calendar bound was the only bound.  Set Module 4's `model_rig_trip_limit = False` for that exactly.","range_high":12.0,"range_low":2.0,"reference_year":2026,"unit":"mining campaigns before wear-out","value":5.0}

A part-worn rig parked on a specific asteroid is worth something to whoever goes there next and nothing to anyone else \u2014 an illiquid, location-locked asset with a market of approximately one buyer.  Half of remaining book value is a deliberately unheroic haircut.  The one space-asset salvage estimate on record brackets it: NASA CR-3349 (1980) puts a solar power satellite's average salvage value at 5-10% of its capital cost, and a demonstration satellite's at 60-90% of its on-orbit cost.  Those are fractions of cost; this one is of remaining book value.  Set 0.0 to model abandonment.","range_high":0.8,"range_low":0.0,"reference_year":2026,"unit":"fraction of remaining book value recoverable","value":0.5}

{"category":"In-space processing plant throughput","notes":"v1.7.0.  Sizes the refinery that turns raw asteroid feedstock into something a depot can actually build with.  Terrestrial smelters run 1,000x their own mass per year (no source is given for this); 100x is a heavy derating for microgravity, no convection, no gravity-fed materials handling and full autonomy.  NASA's only published designs for in-space processing hardware run far lower: 7.28 kg per year per kg (a lunar water plant, Kleinhenz & Paz 2021, NTRS 20210016820) to 13.3 (a Mars propellant plant, Kleinhenz & Paz 2017, AIAA 2017-0423), the band of 'ISRU propellant plant throughput'.  This row's 100 is 7.5 to 14 times that, and its 20 floor is 1.5 times the top.  Nothing here shows why a mineral refinery should outrun ISRU hardware by that much; the value is an estimate. Sizes the plant that electrolyses mined water and liquefies the products, for a propellant whose isru_processing_wh_per_kg is above zero (hydrolox). Let ve=Isp*g0, Rd=exp(departure_dv/ve), Rc=exp(capture_dv/ve), B=exp(lambda*return_cruise_years), and M be dry-return+TPS+cargo+retained tank mass after capture. Capture needs (Rc-1)*M at arrival, thus B*(Rc-1)*M immediately after the departure burn. Required departure fuel is [Rd*(1+B*(Rc-1))-1]*M. The old combined-burn book uses (Rd*Rc-1)*M. Their positive difference for B>1,Rc>1 is Rd*(B-1)*(Rc-1)*M. With old tank mass held fixed this is an optimistic lower bound. For tank mass t*P, fixed non-tank mass S and predeparture storage factor H, exact loaded fuel is H*K*S/(1-t*H*K), K=Rd*(1+B*(Rc-1))-1, where the denominator must stay positive.
